verified.name: ArtiFixer (NVIDIA, SIGGRAPH 2026), 1.3B causal autoregressive variant (Wan2.1-based)
verified.license: The code is Apache-2.0 (gh SPDX check). The weights use the NVIDIA OneWay Noncommercial License (22Mar2022), and the model card says "for research and development only". A maintainer confirmed this split in issue #8. The Wan2.1 base (VAE and T5) is Apache-2.0. The Cosmos3-Nano base is Open MDW 1.1. This is fine for an academic paper and demo, but not for a commercial product.
verified.inputs_match_ours:
Partly. The model wants rendered RGB, a rendered opacity (alpha) map, camera ray maps from intrinsics and poses, real reference views (up to 12 by default), and a T5 caption embedding. gsplat produces RGB and alpha, and ARKit gives the poses and intrinsics, so the core inputs exist. A maintainer said in issue #1 that the model should work with gsplat renders, but the end-to-end scripts assume COLMAP plus 3DGRUT.

The scripts as written need three things we don't have:
- `prepare_colmap_artifixer_inputs` needs a COLMAP `sparse/0` folder. It trains its own 3DGRUT for 10k iterations, runs MoGe for scale, and runs a Qwen3-VL captioner plus T5. We would need to write our own `split.json` and render-dir adapter, or write ARKit poses out as a COLMAP model and pass our own checkpoint via `--reconstruction_checkpoint`, though that flag expects a 3DGRUT checkpoint. `--trajectory_path` accepts a transforms-style JSON (OpenGL c2w, per-frame intrinsics, fixed resolution), which matches a novel path.
- It ignores our LiDAR depth and confidence entirely. Metric scale from ARKit replaces MoGe.
- It is out of distribution for our scans. The model was trained on deliberately sparse 3DGUT reconstructions (2-12 cameras per sample). In issue #10, a user who initialized from dense LiDAR said the rendered opacity was saturated and the fixer "barely works". The maintainer replied that dense LiDAR-supervised splats differ from the training distribution. Our instant LiDAR-surfel splat and the 60-300-frame 80 s splat are exactly that case. Opacity mixing starts generation from the render wherever alpha is about 1, so floaters and smears in fully opaque regions may get only mild correction.
verified.measured_or_reported_speed:
These are reported figures only; I measured nothing. The model card gives 34.38 FPS for the 1.3B model (4 steps, one GPU) and 8.36 FPS for the 14B. The 1.3B reaches 101.77 FPS with 1 step and 4-GPU context parallelism. The card does not state resolution or whether VAE decode, model load and caption prep are included.

Real end-to-end cost per room is much higher:
- **Loading:** the FP32 checkpoints are memory-mapped. The 1.3B file is 6.7 GB (the candidate's 3.4 GB is the BF16 in-memory size). The fp32 construction step spikes host RAM.
- **Per-scene prep:** the captioner (Qwen3-VL-4B or 30B) and the T5 encoder (about 23 GB download) run once per scene. The stock prep also trains 3DGRUT for 10k iterations, which we would bypass.
- **Pipeline shape:** `run_inference` is an offline batch script that writes PNGs and MP4s. The repo has no streaming or server path; the tree search found no stream, server or realtime code. Blocks are 7 latent frames, so latency per chunk is about 1 s even at high throughput.

A 1 s clip for rung 1 is plausible in seconds once everything is warm on an H100. The 30 fps live stream for rung 3 would need serious engineering.
verified.runnable_on_modal:
Yes, with effort. Public prebuilt images exist (`ghcr.io/nv-tlabs/artifixer:cuda12-ffmpeg-free-20261021-5b1bb939`, which includes 3DGRUT; FFmpeg must be added at runtime). Users report building the image yourself takes 1-1.5 h because of FlashAttention-3, so pull the prebuilt one. Plan on about 160 GB of disk for the image, checkpoint and captioner, so cache them on a Modal Volume.

VRAM figures from the issues:
- 14B: a maintainer measured a 35.8 GiB peak on a DL3DV scene. Users hit OOM on a 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 for long clips, because full-clip I/O tensors stay on the GPU. The community fix is to move those tensors to the CPU and turn on VAE tiling.
- 1.3B: should fit on an L40S, A100 or H100 for short clips. A 1 s clip of 30 frames is short.
- Captioner: use the 4B captioner, since the default 30B needs about 60 GB.

The A100 runs on SDPA (no FA3), so for speed use an H100.
verified.gotchas:
1. **Weak fidelity.** On DL3DV the 1.3B scores only about 19.3 PSNR / 0.667 SSIM / 0.265 LPIPS, and about 19.1 / 0.629 / 0.332 for novel content. With 6 views on Mip-NeRF 360 it scores 18.2 PSNR. It is generative, so unobserved regions are hallucinated, which hurts our frame-by-frame comparison against held-out real footage.
2. **Out of distribution.** It was trained on sparse 3DGUT renders. The issue #10 report says dense LiDAR-initialized splats give saturated opacity and the model barely corrects, and that is exactly our input.
3. **Missing adapters and offline-only.** There is no gsplat/ARKit adapter: `split.json`, render dirs, captions and T5 embeddings must all be produced by our own code. Every new scene needs a caption pass. Inference is offline only, with no streaming API.
4. **Noncommercial weights.**
5. **Rung 3 conflicts with the viewer.** Using it for rung 3 means server-rendered video over WebRTC instead of Spark in the browser, which conflicts with "browser stays the viewer". ArtiFixer3D (baking fixes back into a splat) means retraining 3DGRUT, so it is minutes per room, not seconds.
6. **Open issues.** Issue #16 reports that black-mode or reference-only generation drifts far from the reference frames. Issue #12 has many OOM and setup-pain reports. The repo is new: created 2026-06, last push 2026-10-22, 719 stars, maintainers active.
7. **Resolution.** The Wan path snaps to multiples of 16 at native size, so we must downscale our 1920x1440 frames (to about 1024x768) before prep or memory blows up.
8. **Unconfirmed claim.** The candidate's figure of about 9 GB of KV cache for the 1.3B is an estimate derived from the docs' "4.5x less" statement, not a measurement.
verified.verdict: maybe. It is the most complete open fixer for rung 1: real code, ungated weights and Docker images, usable for research. Run it as an offline baseline on a novel path over our gsplat renders. Expect only modest gains on dense LiDAR splats (out of distribution, saturated opacity) and generative hallucination that hurts geometric accuracy. It is not a drop-in for rung 3 live streaming, and the license is noncommercial.

verified.name: Spark 2.4.0 (sparkjsdev/spark): three.js Gaussian splat renderer with streamed level-of-detail (.RAD files) and runtime editing of splat objects
verified.license: MIT for the JS and the Rust code. Changelog 2.2.0 fixed a missing license on the Rust part (#422). Fine for commercial use.
verified.inputs_match_ours: Partly. Spark only renders and edits splats. It loads our gsplat .ply/.spz (and .sog, .ksplat, .RAD). It never sees our scan data: the camera poses, LiDAR depth, confidence and RoomPlan layout. It cannot split an object out of the room. For rung 2 we must cut the object out ourselves, for example by selecting splats inside the RoomPlan object box and saving them as a separate splat file. Spark can then hide that box in the room (an inverted box shape edit with opacity 0) and move the object with its own transform. Nothing fills the hole the object leaves behind.
verified.measured_or_reported_speed: Not benchmarked by me. Vendor docs give splat budgets: iPhone 1-3M splats, Android phone 1-2M, Quest 3 at most 1M, computer 1-5M (10-20M+ on some desktops). Above about 1M splats, per-splat processing becomes the bottleneck on some systems. Building the level-of-detail tree in the browser takes 1-3 s per 1M splats, in a background worker. The build-lod tool is Rust (cargo build --release, optional wgpu GPU feature). Its default --quick mode is fast, and --quality is slower and recommended for streaming. A single room trained by gsplat for 1250 steps is probably at most about 1-2M splats, so it fits the budget even without level of detail.
verified.runnable_on_modal: The viewer runs on the client, not on Modal. build-lod is a native Rust command-line tool, so it runs in a Linux Modal image with rustup (no GPU needed; wgpu is an optional feature). One install report (#489) failed on the Rust Cargo.toml license field. The maintainers point to the user's environment, but we should pin the Rust toolchain. For a one-room scene we can skip build-lod and let the browser build the tree, or use no level of detail at all.
verified.gotchas:
Checked facts: 3,939 stars, MIT, not archived, last push 2026-11-19. Releases: v2.0.0 (2026-04-14), 2.1.0, 2.2.0 (2026-09-11), 2.3.0/2.3.1, v2.4.0 (2026-10-20); npm latest is 2.4.0. The docs confirm build-lod (--quick/--quality/--rad-chunked/--max-sh) and paged .RAD streaming. Reasons it will not do what the candidate claims:
(1) It does nothing for rung 1. Floaters, streaks and the smeared floor come from training, not the renderer. Spark will not raise PSNR, SSIM or LPIPS against the held-out phone clip, so this is plumbing, not a quality fix.
(2) Our metrics may not match what users see. Rung 1 scores are computed from gsplat renders, while Spark rasterizes differently (its own 2D blur and antialiasing, sqrt(8)-sigma footprint, per-splat sort, SH precision fixes in 2.4.0). Either render the evaluation frames from Spark itself (for example a headless browser at the clip's camera intrinsics and poses) or report both.
(3) Object moves lag the camera. Splat updates are asynchronous, so a moved SplatMesh shows up one or more frames after the camera has moved (#205, still open; maintainer: "inherent limitation"). The workaround is SparkRenderer's preUpdate option, which costs speed. This affects rung 2 and the rung 4 transform sync.
(4) Click picking on an edited room is wrong. Raycasts ignore SplatEdits: splats we hid are still hit, and displaced splats are hit where they used to be (#497, opened 2026-11-12). Picking objects in a room with one cut out needs our own approach.
(5) Level of detail supports one camera only (#369). Several SparkRenderers sharing paged meshes fight over level-of-detail state. Per-client rendering for rung 4 is fine, but picture-in-picture or several views inside one client with .RAD files is not.
(6) Stutter. On Chrome on M-series Macs, splats jump each time a sort finishes (#407, open). That matters for "30 fps while walking" on Macs, which a video call likely includes. 2.4.0 fixed stutter during animation (#347/#460); worth re-testing.
(7) iOS streaming freeze. On iOS in WebXR, .RAD streaming hard-freezes with buffered worker decoding (#481, open, 2026-10-11).
(8) Other open issues: Firefox on Windows is orders of magnitude slower (#190); WASM CompileError on Android Firefox (#362); no reliable "paged file ready" event (#364, #317), so the moment to start a synced timeline is unclear; getBoundingBox grows non-deterministically for .RAD (#373); sort buffers never shrink after one large view (#499).
(9) No networking. Rung 4 sync (camera poses, object transforms) must be built ourselves, for example over a WebRTC data channel or a CRDT library such as Yjs. The candidate's note that no open multi-user browser splat system exists was not re-verified here.
(10) Level of detail is mostly unnecessary for one room. .RAD paging pays off for large worlds; a room of 1-2M splats fits the phone budget. The real win from build-lod is faster first load: streaming a chunked .RAD lets people start viewing before the whole file arrives.
verified.verdict: use: keep it as the viewer and upgrade to 2.4.0. It is MIT, actively maintained and already in our stack, with confirmed support for transforms, multiple objects and .RAD streaming. It does nothing for rung 1 quality. Plan workarounds for the frame lag when moving objects (#205, use preUpdate), raycasts that ignore edits (#497), single-camera level of detail (#369), Chrome-on-Mac sort stutter (#407) and the iOS streaming freeze (#481). Write the multi-user sync layer ourselves.

verified.name: NVIDIA Fixer (nv-tlabs/Fixer + nvidia/Fixer, Cosmos-Predict2 0.6B single-step fixer)
verified.license: Code is Apache-2.0 (confirmed with gh). Weights use the NVIDIA Open Model License: the HF cardData has license_name nvidia-open-model-license, and the card says "ready for commercial/non-commercial use". The weights are ungated (gated=false). Two strings attached: (1) the base runtime image nvcr.io/nvidia/cosmos/cosmos-predict2-container:1.2 needs an NGC login (issue #5 hit a 401 on docker build), so someone needs a free NGC account and API key, and that is a step for the user, not us; (2) the NVIDIA OML has its own terms (guardrail clauses, attribution), so it is not an OSI license, but it is commercially usable.
verified.inputs_match_ours: Partly. The input is one RGB image and nothing else: no pose, depth or reference view. Inference runs at fixed 16:9 sizes only (get_resolution_size maps 256/512/704/960/1024/1360 to widths of 256x144 up to 1360x768, with 1024x576 the trained default). Our 4:3 frames (1920x1440) would need cropping or letterboxing, or a finetune at a 4:3 size. It ignores our metric depth, poses and the real ARKit photos we already have. Issue #4 (open) confirms: "Fixer does not support image input at the moment", so there is no reference-view conditioning the way Difix had it, and per-frame multi-view consistency is not anchored. Training data was NVIDIA's internal AV driving dataset (the card's intended domain is ADAS). For indoor rooms we should expect to finetune on pairs of (our gsplat render, held-out ARKit frame), which the included training script supports via --pretrained_path.
verified.measured_or_reported_speed: These are reported numbers only; we have not measured anything. The HF card gives 26.5 ms/frame on H100, 50.6 on A100, 61.7 on H20 and 87.8 on L40, at 576x1024. The code's speed_measure() shows those numbers are model-only (encode, one denoise step, decode), after torch.compile and 50 warmup iterations in bf16 on random tensors. They exclude image I/O, the gsplat render and video encoding. That leaves only about 6 ms of the 33 ms budget for render plus NVENC at 30 fps on an H100, and it means one H100 per live viewpoint. A100 and L40S cannot reach 30 fps at 1024x576. Lower resolutions (704x384, 512x288) are supported and would be faster. TensorRT export is blocked: issue #7 (open) reports that ONNX export fails because the tokenizer ships only as TorchScript, with no source.
verified.runnable_on_modal: Probably, with work. Option A: use the nvcr cosmos-predict2-container:1.2 image as a Modal registry image, with an NGC API key stored as a Modal secret. Option B: rebuild the environment from source (pip cosmos-predict2==1.0.9 --no-deps, plus transformer_engine, lpips, vision-aided-loss and CLIP), which is the fragile path. The weights are about 5.5 GB (pretrained_fixer.pkl 4.05 GB, model_fast_tokenizer.pt 1.2 GB, tokenizer_fast.pth 0.23 GB), so cache them in a Modal Volume. The code hardcodes /work/models/base/... paths. Memory is fine on any of H100, A100 or L40S. The checkpoint loads through torch.load of a .pkl, which is pickle; acceptable because it is NVIDIA's own HF repo.
verified.gotchas: 1) No reference-image conditioning (issue #4), so each frame is fixed independently. Expect temporal flicker on a 1 s novel-path video and hallucinated detail that can lower PSNR against the real held-out clip, even when LPIPS improves. 2) AV-only training data, so domain shift on indoor rooms is likely and a finetune will probably be needed (the repo's example is 8-GPU accelerate for 10k steps, though batch size 1 should also work on fewer GPUs). 3) Fixed 16:9 resolutions against our 4:3 captures. 4) NGC login is needed for the container. 5) No TensorRT path (TorchScript tokenizer; issue #7 is unresolved). 6) Small, quiet repo: 166 stars, last pushed 2026-07-30, 5 open issues, maintainers answer rarely. 7) The 26.5 ms figure excludes the rest of the live pipeline, so 30 fps on an H100 is borderline and A100/L40S are out. 8) The model card says DC-AE, but the code uses a Cosmos 16-channel 8x tokenizer; this does not matter in practice. Confirmed URLs: https://github.com/nv-tlabs/Fixer, https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Fixer (the older SD-based version with a reference input is https://huggingface.co/nvidia/difix).
verified.verdict: use: it has the best license of the fixers, the code and weights are real, ungated and complete, and it is the only one with credible about-30 ms speed. Adopt it first for offline Difix3D+-style pseudo-view cleanup inside our gsplat training (rungs 1-2). Treat live 30 fps (rung 3) as unproven until we measure the whole pipeline on an H100. Plan an indoor finetune, and add temporal or reference anchoring ourselves, because it has neither.

verified.name: Difix / Difix-ref (Difix3D+, CVPR 2025 Oral), nv-tlabs/Difix3D
verified.license: The code and weights are under the NVIDIA License. Section 3.3 of LICENSE.txt says the Work and any derivative works may be used "non-commercially", meaning research or evaluation only, and NVIDIA keeps commercial rights for itself. The same LICENSE.txt also carries the Stability AI Community License for the SD-Turbo base, which bans commercial use above $1M revenue and requires "Powered by Stability AI" attribution. This is fine for a research paper and demo, but we cannot ship it in a product. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION. The successor, nv-tlabs/Fixer, is Apache-2.0 for code (166 stars, pushed 2026-07-30); I did not check the license on Fixer's weights.
verified.inputs_match_ours: Partly. It needs one rendered RGB frame, plus one reference RGB image for difix_ref (the nearest training view by pose). It ignores our metric LiDAR depth, confidence maps, RoomPlan layout and intrinsics. Poses are used only to pick the reference view. It accepts exactly one reference image: issue #41 asks for multiple references and issue #47 shows the quality drops when the reference view is far off. That is the normal case for our thin scans on a new camera path. The model was trained at about 512 to 576x1024, so our 1920x1440 renders need to be downscaled (or tiled). It was trained on DL3DV, Nerfbusters and in-house driving data, with no ScanNet++ and no indoor-specific results reported, though DL3DV does include some indoor scenes.
verified.measured_or_reported_speed: The paper reports "the additional rendering time is only 76 ms on an NVIDIA A100 GPU" (Sec. 4.2), but it does not state the resolution. Users could not reproduce this. In issue #21, a 1920x1080 frame on an A100 with the diffusers pipeline took about 1.4 s in fp32 and 0.8 s in fp16, scaling roughly linearly with pixel count. NVIDIA never answered. Extrapolating, about 576x1024 in fp16 is about 0.2 s per frame on an A100, maybe 0.1 to 0.15 s on an H100. That is roughly 5 to 10 fps before streaming overhead, not 15 to 25 fps. The 76 ms figure only holds at small resolution or with an optimized TensorRT path that is not released. The Difix3D+ distillation in the shipped gsplat example (examples/gsplat/simple_trainer_difix3d.py) runs Difix at fix_steps every 2k iterations up to 60k steps, re-rendering and fixing every novel pose each time. That takes many minutes, against our 1250 steps and 80 s, and issue #33 calls it "not real time". Training a new Difix needs 32 GB or more of VRAM at 576x1024 (maintainer, issue #13). Inference fits easily on an L40S, A100 or H100.
verified.runnable_on_modal: Yes, for inference. It loads through diffusers DifixPipeline.from_pretrained('nvidia/difix_ref', trust_remote_code=True). Both HF repos are ungated and were updated 2026-07-21: nvidia/difix_ref has 18.8k downloads and nvidia/difix has 5k. The catch is old pins in requirements.txt: diffusers==0.25.1, transformers==4.38.0, peft==0.9.0, huggingface-hub==0.25.1 and xformers. These may clash with our gsplat 1.5.3 / torch image, so it should get its own Modal image. Issues #50 (FromOriginalVAEMixin ImportError) and #45 (the custom AutoencoderKL needs a local import to load) show breakage on newer diffusers. Also remember to call .to('cuda') and disable the progress bar; issue #33's slowness came from forgetting these.
verified.gotchas: 1) The maintainers have deprecated it. Issue #67, posted by Florian Hofherr: "DiFix is a previous-generation model. Its newer, supported version is Fixer". The Difix3D repo was last pushed 2025-06-28 and is "maintained on a best-effort basis". 2) Several users found the Difix3D+ distillation made metrics worse. In issue #40, gsplat PSNR dropped from about 28.5 to 26.7, and others report "sometimes it becomes even worse". Issue #56 reports "oddly colored blocks" on custom and VGGT-based data. 3) The paper's own DL3DV gains are mostly perceptual: FID improves from 107 to 41, but PSNR only from 17.18 to 17.99. Our rung-1 score is PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS against a held-out phone clip, and generative hallucinations can lower PSNR and SSIM even while they look better. 4) Running it on every frame without the 3D distillation flickers; the paper admits this ("causes flickering"). That is bad for rung 3's live 30 fps. 5) It only takes a single reference image and degrades when that reference is far from the new view, which is exactly the thin-scan failure case. 6) The 76 ms speed claim is unreproduced at real resolutions (issue #21). 7) The license is non-commercial, on top of the SD-Turbo community license. 8) Old diffusers pins and remote code. 9) Rung 2 (moved object): the fixer copies the nearest reference image, which shows the object in its old place, so it may pull the render back toward the stale view.
verified.verdict: Maybe. It is the cheapest drop-in baseline for rung 1 (render the new path, run difix_ref with the nearest scan frame, score it), since weights are ungated and the API is 3 lines. But NVIDIA has deprecated it in favour of Fixer (whose code is Apache-2.0), the license is non-commercial, real speed is about 0.2 s per frame at 576x1024 rather than 76 ms, the distillation is minutes long and sometimes lowers PSNR, and single-frame use flickers. Use it as a quick comparison point, but put the main effort into Fixer.

verified.name: NVIDIA GEN3C (Cosmos-Predict1-7B, 3D-cache-conditioned video)
verified.license: Code is Apache-2.0 (confirmed via gh). The GEN3C weights use the NVIDIA Open Model License, which allows commercial use (stated in the README). Other weights the download script pulls: Cosmos-Tokenize1-CV8x8x8-720p (HF license "other", now ungated: gated=False, which corrects the candidate's claim that it is gated) and google-t5/t5-11b (Apache-2.0, ungated). Optional extras: Cosmos-Guardrail1 (HF gated=auto) and Llama-Guard-3-8B (gated=manual). You can skip both with --disable_guardrail. The Pixtral-12B prompt upsampler is ungated and optional (--disable_prompt_upsampler).
verified.inputs_match_ours: Mostly yes. gen3c_multiview.py reads an npz with these keys: images_key_frames (N,3,H,W in [-1,1]), depth_key_frames (N,1,H,W, metric, must be in the same scale as the poses), mask_key_frames (we can fill this from LiDAR confidence), K_key_frames (OpenCV convention), w2cs_key_frames (world-to-camera), w2cs_all (ANY custom target path, one 4x4 per frame) and an optional Ks_all. So ARKit poses, ARKit intrinsics and upsampled LiDAR depth plug in directly, and the held-out clip's camera path can go in as w2cs_all. No ViPE/VGGT step is needed. Mismatches: (1) ARKit gives camera-to-world in OpenGL axes. You must invert it and flip the axes to OpenCV w2c. Issue #47 is someone who got wrong output from exactly this mistake. (2) The model only runs at 1280x704 (16:9). Issue #53 hits shape errors at other sizes. Our 1920x1440 (4:3) frames must be cropped or padded, and scoring has to use the same crop of the real clip. (3) Clips are always 121 frames (or 120N+1). For a 1-second, 30-frame clip, interpolate the path to 121 poses and keep every 4th frame, or generate a longer path. (4) We cannot feed it our whole LiDAR point cloud or all 60-300 frames. The Cache3D_BufferSelector in cache_3d.py hard-codes frame_buffer_max=2 and picks the top-2 keyframes by overlap summed over the WHOLE 121-frame chunk, not per frame. A path through the room is therefore conditioned on only 2 scan views per chunk. Issue #26 confirms the released model handles at most 2 buffers. (5) It uses num_input_frames=1, and the seed image is images_key_frames[0]. Output frame 0 is anchored to keyframe 0's image, so the target path must start at keyframe 0's pose. Otherwise frame 0 comes out wrong. For a fair held-out test, start the path at the nearest scan keyframe, or synthesize a seed frame (for example render it from the splat). (6) Upsampling 256x192 LiDAR depth to 704x1280 blurs depth edges. Use the confidence mask and --filter_points_threshold to cut flying pixels.
verified.measured_or_reported_speed: Not measured by us. Two independent reports put it at about 15 minutes per 121-frame clip on one A100: issue #33, where a maintainer (xrenaa) confirmed the speed problem and said it needs distillation to get faster, and the OutofAi/GEN3C-MODAL README (Apache-2.0, 4 stars, last pushed 2025-12-01). It uses 35 diffusion steps by default. The official README has 8-GPU torchrun context parallelism but no timing table. Our estimate is roughly 8-12 min on one H100 and about 2-3 min on 8 H100s per chunk. A 1-second clip costs as much as a full 121-frame chunk. Nowhere near real time.
verified.runnable_on_modal: Yes, for offline batch jobs. Tested only on H100/A100. Peak memory is about 43 GB with every offload flag, so one H100-80GB or A100-80GB works. L40S (48 GB) is borderline. Blackwell needs a community NGC Docker fork (issue #37). Checkpoints are large: GEN3C model.pt is 28.9 GB (HF usedStorage), and t5-11b alone is about 45 GB. The checksum list also references tf_model.h5, so the download may be about 90 GB. Cache everything in a Modal Volume. Install uses the Cosmos-Predict1 conda environment plus apex/transformer-engine, and past issues report install trouble (#13 apex amp_C, #12 retinaface). Use the repo Dockerfile as the Modal image base. A community Modal port (OutofAi/GEN3C-MODAL) exists and can serve as a reference.
verified.gotchas: 1) The released model uses at most 2 buffer views, chosen once per 121-frame chunk. A long path through a thin scan sees only 2 keyframes per chunk, so everything else in the room gets hallucinated. Plan paths short enough for 2 views to cover them, or split them into chunks. 2) Output frame 0 is pinned to keyframe 0's image (num_input_frames=1). This complicates scoring a held-out path frame by frame. 3) Locked to 1280x704 at 16:9, so our 4:3 frames must be cropped or padded. 4) Pose convention traps: it needs OpenCV w2c, and ARKit gives OpenGL c2w (issues #47 and #55; also #46 reports a bug in look_at_matrix). 5) About 15 min per clip on an A100 rules it out for rungs 3-4 and for "seconds from capture". 6) No training or fine-tuning code has been released (#29, #61). 7) Moving an object for rung 2 is not built in. The multiview path never updates the cache ("No cache update"), so we would edit the depth, mask and image buffers ourselves, and the 2-buffer limit still applies. 8) Last push to the repo was 2026-06-15, with 33 open issues and no maintainer replies on recent ones. Community work is moving to Cosmos-Predict2.5/cosmos-framework (#57, 2026-08). Lyra (nv-tlabs/lyra, distils GEN3C into feed-forward 3DGS) is the faster sibling to look at. 9) ZeroGPU HF Spaces exist (alexnasa/GEN3C-ZEROGPU), which is useful for a quick smoke test of quality before spending on Modal. 10) Multiview custom-data conversion has no official script. Issue #45 is open asking for one, and the community fork dsvilarkovic/GEN3C README_MULTIVIEW is the reference.
verified.verdict: use for rung 1 only, as the offline Modal H100 'gold' renderer and a source of pseudo-ground-truth views. Code, ungated weights and a custom-path w2cs_all input are all confirmed, and ARKit poses plus LiDAR depth drop straight in. Within a 121-frame chunk it is limited to 2 keyframes, and each clip takes about 10-15 min, so it cannot serve rungs 3-4.

verified.name: WorldMirror 2.0 (HY-World-2.0 world reconstruction)
verified.license: Tencent HY-World 2.0 Community License (custom; GitHub shows NOASSERTION). I read License.txt. It does not apply in the EU, UK or South Korea, and any use or display of the model or its outputs there is unlicensed. Organisations with more than 1M MAU on the release date must ask Tencent for a license. Clause 5b bans using the model's output to improve any other AI model. A per-room gsplat fine-tune is probably fine, but distilling into our own feed-forward net is not. v1 (HunyuanWorld-Mirror) has a separate license with the same territory clause.
verified.inputs_match_ours: Partly. The prior format is what the candidate described: prior_cam_path is a JSON of c2w poses in OpenCV convention (ARKit is OpenGL-style, so the axes need flipping) plus K at the original resolution. prior_depth_path holds .npy/.exr/16-bit png files matched by filename, and small depth maps are bilinearly upsampled. But I read the code (worldmirror.py extract_priors, priors.py), and the priors only condition the network; they do not carry metric scale. (1) normalize_depth() rescales EACH view's depth on its own to [0,1] using the 1st-99th percentiles. That throws away the LiDAR metric scale and the scale agreement between views. A maintainer confirmed this in v1 issue #36 ("does not support metric-scale prediction... scale information is missing") and suggested a RANSAC scale fit afterwards. (2) normalize_poses() squeezes the camera positions into a unit cube, after pipeline.py has re-expressed every pose relative to view 0. (3) The pipeline never maps its output back into the prior frame. gaussians.ply comes out in the model's own frame, anchored at camera 0 and at an arbitrary scale, so it is NOT in ARKit/MuJoCo world coordinates. We must fit a Sim(3) from the predicted cameras to the ARKit poses (Umeyama) ourselves. (4) The LiDAR confidence maps are not used, and the zero (invalid) pixels get blurred into valid ones by the bilinear upsample. (5) The 60-300 frames have to be cut to about 32-64 views.
verified.measured_or_reported_speed: Reported only, not measured by me. Tech report Table 14 (H20, BF16, 378x518): 32 views 2.1 s / 15 GB, 64 views 5.7 s / 25 GB, 128 views 17 s / 42 GB. The pipeline's default target_size is 952, which makes about 3.5x more tokens per view than those benchmarks (68x51 patches vs 27x37). Expect 32 views at 952 to cost roughly what 128 views do at 518. An H100 has much more BF16 compute than an H20, so it should be faster, but no H100 numbers have been published. Saving takes extra time on top of that: masks, ONNX sky segmentation, voxel pruning of up to S*H*W Gaussians, and the PLY write. Expect a few seconds to about 20 s per room, not under a second, and nowhere near 30 fps re-inference.
verified.runnable_on_modal: Yes, probably. The environment is fixed: torch 2.7.1, CUDA 12.8 recommended, Python 3.11, open3d 0.18, pycolmap 3.10. requirements_git.txt builds pytorch3d, MoGe, fused-ssim, nerfview and spz from source, which makes a heavy image. The worldrecon part alone probably needs less, but I did not check that. The 1.2B model fits on a single H100 or A100-80GB; L40S (48 GB) only works at lower resolution or with fewer views. Multi-GPU via torchrun/FSDP is supported. Note v2 issue #1: one user reports a 160 GB peak for the full generation pipeline, but that figure is for worldgen, not worldrecon.
verified.gotchas: 1) Not metric, not in our world frame. Depth priors are normalized per view, poses are re-anchored to view 0 and squeezed into a unit cube, and the output is never transformed back. We must Sim(3)-align the predicted cameras to ARKit (or scale-fit the predicted depth to LiDAR) before putting it in Spark or MuJoCo. 2) The exported gaussians.ply probably renders wrongly in Spark. The opacities are already sigmoid-activated (act_gs.reg_dense_opacities) but are written raw into the 'opacity' field, where standard 3DGS viewers expect logits. On top of that, _voxel_prune_gaussians sets the merged opacity from the weights (scatter_add of w*w / wsum) and never reads the actual opacities (open issue #34, unanswered). This may explain v1 issues #40 and #43, where the internal render videos look fine but the PLY looks bad in SuperSplat. We should export from predictions['splats'] ourselves, writing logit(opacity). 3) SH degree 0 only, so there is no view-dependent color. 4) The voxel prune size of 0.002 and the depth-edge thresholds are in the model's arbitrary units. 5) The Gaussians are pixel-aligned, one per pixel per view (12M+ before pruning), so the method interpolates and does not fill unseen regions. The maintainers say themselves that extrapolated views degrade (v1 #40), v2 issue #5 reports holes and no completion in the output, and the paper's NVS is about 20 PSNR without priors. That is exactly our failure mode: new camera paths after a thin scan. 6) v1 #39 and #32: several users found that adding COLMAP poses/intrinsics made results WORSE. The prior conventions are tricky, and the old README had wrong key names. 7) No v2 training code (issue #32 open), so we cannot fine-tune the network on ARKit data. v1 does ship training code and a gsplat post-optimization script (submodules/gsplat/examples/simple_trainer_worldmirror.py); v2 has a world_gs_trainer.py, but only in worldgen. 8) The license blocks EU/UK/KR users and outputs, which matters for a multi-user browser product if any participant is there. 9) v1 #40: a user found AnySplat's PLY clearly better than WorldMirror's on the same inputs, so benchmark against AnySplat and our LiDAR-surfel instant splat before committing.
verified.verdict: maybe. The code, ungated weights (HY-WorldMirror-2.0/model.safetensors) and pose/intrinsics/depth prior inputs are real, and it is maintained (pushed 2026-08). But the priors do not carry metric scale or our world frame: depth is normalized per view, poses are re-normalized, and the output stays in the model's own frame. The exported PLY opacity looks wrong for standard viewers, quality drops on extrapolated views (our main failure case), and the license excludes the EU, UK and South Korea. Worth a 1-day Modal test as a seed for a short gsplat fine-tune, using our own export, a Sim(3) alignment to ARKit and an A/B against the LiDAR-surfel splat. Not a drop-in fix for rung 1.

verified.name: FastGS (CVPR 2026), github.com/fastgs/FastGS
verified.license: Mixed. The repo's license field is MIT, but it also ships LICENSE_ORIGINAL.md (the Inria 3DGS license, non-commercial). The training code is a fork of Inria 3DGS. The rasterizer it vendors (submodules/diff-gaussian-rasterization_fastgs, a directory, not a git submodule) is Inria-derived plus Taming-3DGS and Speedy-Splat code. Treat it as research-only. The algorithm is small enough to re-implement cleanly on gsplat (Apache-2.0). HF Goodsleepeverday/fastgs is MIT, but it only holds pretrained benchmark scenes, which we don't need.
verified.inputs_match_ours: Partly. It loads only COLMAP sparse models or Blender-style transforms_train.json/test.json (scene/dataset_readers.py), so ARKit poses must be exported to one of those, and LiDAR points or surfels can stand in for the initial point cloud. It uses no depth at all: no depth loss and no depth-guided densification, so our metric LiDAR depth and confidence go unused. The issue tracker shows no ARKit or iPhone use. Default resolution is capped at 1.6K width, which is fine for 1920x1440.
verified.measured_or_reported_speed: Reported, not measured by me: about 100 s per scene for the full 30k-iteration schedule on an RTX 4090. The speed comes mainly from keeping very few Gaussians, not from fewer steps. Every scene in train_base.sh still runs 30k iterations, with densification every 500. On an H100 with ~150 iPhone frames I'd expect a similar order of magnitude, but nothing confirms it. Overhead of the multi-view score is 10 random cameras x 2 renders per densification step, which is small.
verified.runnable_on_modal: Yes, but expect friction. You need a custom image that compiles the CUDA extension. The authors tested on nvcc 11.8 / conda CUDA 11.6 and recommend 24 GB. Issue #7, still open (18 comments): random "illegal memory access" errors in the fastgs rasterizer on CUDA 12.8+/PyTorch 2.9 and on RTX 50xx and 3090. The authors only vouch for the 4090 + cu11.8 setup, and H100 (sm_90) on new CUDA is untested. Issue #58 (closed) is a related crash in the compact-box code when opacity < 1/255. The safer route is a port to our existing gsplat 1.5.3 trainer.
verified.gotchas: 1) There is no gsplat backend. gsplat issue #841 and FastGS issue #21 (open, 9 comments) both ask for one, and the authors say they are "looking into it", but no port exists. To copy the idea we write it ourselves. The core, compute_gaussian_score_fastgs in utils/fast_utils.py, is about 60 lines: render 10 sampled views, threshold the normalised L1 map at loss_thresh, then count per Gaussian how many views it hits flagged pixels in. In stock FastGS that count comes from a custom rasterizer output (accum_metric_counts). In gsplat it could be rebuilt with rasterize_to_indices_in_range, or with a gradient trick. 2) Issue #57 matters for us: the authors say their random camera sampling "may not work well" for walk-through scenes where images rarely share Gaussians, and they never tested such scenes. That is exactly a thin room scan. We'd need to sample cameras whose frusta overlap, using the ARKit poses. 3) It is a speed method with "comparable" quality. It densifies only where several views agree the error is high and prunes aggressively. That cuts the Gaussian count but adds no prior for unseen views, so it won't by itself fix floaters or a smeared floor from barely-seen viewpoints, and it can under-fit regions only one view covers. 4) Hyperparameters are tuned per scene (issues #50 and #41: grad_abs_thresh, loss_thresh, highfeature_lr, dense, mult), with no general guidance beyond "lower thresholds give more Gaussians". 5) The sparse-view result comes from the Fast-DropGaussian branch, built on DropGaussian (a few-shot benchmark setup), not from FastGS alone. 6) The candidate's category "slam" is wrong. The Photo-SLAM branch is still unreleased (issue #33), and none of rungs 2-4 (moved objects, 30 fps live, multi-user) are addressed. 7) The repo is maintained (last push 2026-03-23, 1307 stars, not archived), but most bugs are answered with "use our exact environment.yml".
verified.verdict: maybe: copy the multi-view-consistent densify/prune rule into our gsplat trainer (about 100 lines, with camera sampling by pose overlap instead of at random) to cut Gaussian count and training time. Don't adopt the repo itself: its rasterizer is Inria-licensed and crash-prone on new CUDA, it ignores our LiDAR depth, it is tuned per scene, and it doesn't solve novel-view quality on thin scans.

verified.name: ArtifactWorld (fyting/ArtifactWorld, 3DGS artifact restoration on LTX-Video 13B 0.9.8-distilled, arXiv 2604.12251, ACM MM 2026)
verified.license: The repo code is Apache-2.0, confirmed with gh. The ArtifactWorld LoRAs and auxiliary latents are CC-BY-NC-4.0 and HF-gated with gated='manual', which means approval by hand. I confirmed this with the HF API: weights.tar is about 2.05 GB, lastModified 2026-04-29. The base model is Lightricks LTX-Video (ltxv-13b-0.9.8-distilled.safetensors, confirmed in Lightricks/LTX-Video, plus the 0.9.7-dev scheduler and the 13B VAE). It is not gated, but its license is 'other' (the LTXV open-weights license), not OSI. Overall it is usable for research only, not commercially.
verified.inputs_match_ours: Only partly. The input must be one 960x544, 97-frame clip laid out like this (tools/process_videos.py): frame 0 is a clean GT image of the trajectory's FIRST view, frames 1-87 are the artifact splat render, and frame 88 is a clean GT image of the trajectory's LAST view, repeated for frames 89-96. The clean anchors are meant to be pixel-aligned endpoints of the same path, not loose "nearest reference frames". For us that means every novel path must start and end exactly at captured ARKit scan poses, and we pass those real JPEGs as anchors. For the rung-1 eval, the anchors must not come from the held-out phone clip, or the eval leaks. The model ignores our metric LiDAR depth, poses, intrinsics and confidence, and has no geometry conditioning. Its only text prompt is "remove artifact". Our 1-second clips (about 30 frames) have to be padded or resampled to 97 frames at 960x544, and the output then rescaled to 1920x1440 aspect, which is 4:3 against the model's roughly 16:9. Expect cropping or letterboxing, which hurts PSNR/SSIM.
verified.measured_or_reported_speed: Not reported anywhere: README, paper badge, issues. Not measured; I did not run it. The configs show 8 denoising steps, guidance 1.0, 960x544x97, bf16, run twice in sequence (Stage-1 heatmap LoRA, then Stage-2 restoration LoRA). Inference goes through LTX-Video-Trainer's validate.py, which reloads the T5 encoder, the 13B transformer and the VAE on each call. My estimate for an H100: roughly 20-60 s per clip warm and 2+ minutes cold, which is not "seconds from capture". Users in issue #3 ran it on an RTX A6000 48 GB with no OOM, and on an RTX 4090 24 GB only with CPU offload or INT8.
verified.runnable_on_modal: Yes on paper. An H100-80GB or A100-80GB fits bf16 without offload. An L40S-48GB should fit, based on the A6000 report. You would bake about 30+ GB of weights into a Modal volume: the 13B transformer single file, the T5 encoder, the 13B VAE, the 0.9.7-dev scheduler and the 2 GB LoRA tar. To be fast you would need to write a persistent-warm wrapper that keeps the models loaded, instead of the shell scripts. One blocker is that a human has to request HF access and wait for manual approval. In issue #2, requests took anywhere from days to weeks, and several are still waiting.
verified.gotchas:
1) The release has been fragile. The configs shipped at release loaded the wrong transformer (0.9.7-dev) and the wrong 2B VAE, which gave blurry, tiled or flat-gray output (issues #3, #4, #6). The fixes landed 2026-08-10 (transformer) and 2026-10-29 (VAE, via a community PR). The authors say it works now, but no independent user has confirmed a good result since the VAE fix. Plan on debugging.
2) Fixed input format: 960x544x97 frames, with GT anchors at the first and last frames of the target path (see inputs).
3) It is a generative video model, so it can hallucinate or shift texture and fine geometry. Pixel metrics (PSNR/SSIM) against a real clip may drop even when the result looks better. Geometric accuracy is not guaranteed, only "close to the splat render".
4) It works offline on short clips only. It does nothing for live 30 fps in the browser (rungs 3-4) unless we use its output as pseudo-views to re-fit the splat, which adds minutes.
5) Training code and the 107.5K-clip training data are not released, so we cannot fine-tune on indoor LiDAR scans or change the frame layout.
6) Small project: 31 stars, 2 open issues, last push 2026-10-29. The authors do respond.
7) The NC license blocks any commercial use of LiteReality.
verified.verdict: Maybe. It is real and has runnable inference with downloadable (gated, NC) weights, and it is a reasonable offline cleaner for the rung-1 eval video if paths start and end at scan poses. But the release configs only recently stopped producing garbage, its speed is unmeasured (likely tens of seconds per clip, not seconds), it ignores our depth and poses, and it is research-only. Request HF access now and treat it as an experiment, not the main path.

all.name: ArtiFixer (NVIDIA, SIGGRAPH 2026) - 1.3B causal autoregressive variant
all.what: Autoregressive video diffusion model, built on Wan2.1 or Cosmos3-Nano, that corrects and extends 3DGS renders along a camera path. It is conditioned on real anchor views (up to 12 references) and uses opacity mixing so it can fill holes the scan never saw. ArtiFixer3D distills the corrected frames back into a new 3DGS. ArtiFixer3D+ runs the fixer again on that reconstruction's renders. The repo ships inference, data prep, training (S1 bidirectional, S2 diffusion forcing, S3 self-forcing DMD) and benchmark code.
all.license: Code is Apache-2.0. Weights use the NVIDIA OneWay Noncommercial License, so research and evaluation only. The Wan2.1 base is Apache-2.0 and the Cosmos3-Nano base is Open MDW 1.1.
all.weights: Public and ungated on HF (nvidia/ArtiFixer, updated 2026-10-22): artifixer-1.3b.pt, artifixer-14b.pt, artifixer-cosmos3-nano.pt, plus the S1 bidirectional teachers. The files hold only the transformer; the VAE and T5 come from the Wan-AI/Wan2.1-T2V-*-Diffusers base.
all.inputs: A 3DGS of the scene, posed renders along the target trajectory (it accepts a novel-path trajectory.json with per-frame intrinsics), real anchor frames as references, and a text caption (Qwen3-VL captioner plus T5 embeddings). Their prep script starts from COLMAP and trains its own 3DGRUT for 10k iterations. We would swap in our gsplat renders and ARKit poses, which means writing an adapter for split.json. MoGe is used to estimate metric scale; we can skip it because ARKit gives metric scale.
all.speed: From the model card: the distilled causal 1.3B model runs at 34.38 FPS with 4 denoising steps on one GPU. The 14B runs at 8.36 FPS. The 1.3B reaches up to 101.77 FPS with 1 step and 4-GPU context parallelism. The KV cache works in blocks of 7 latent frames, which I estimate at about 25-28 raw frames (not measured). So expect roughly 1 s of chunk latency even at a high frame rate.
all.gpu: 1.3B: about 3.4 GB of BF16 weights plus a KV cache about 4.5x smaller than the 14B's 40 GB at 1024x576 (so about 9 GB), plus about 0.4 GB per reference view. That fits an L40S, A100 or H100. 14B: about 79-89 GB at 960x544, so it needs an H100 80GB. Caption prep also pulls a 23 GB T5 encoder, and the default 30B captioner needs about 60 GB; the 4B captioner is an option. Docker images are published on ghcr.
all.fit: The best match for rungs 1 and 3. Rung 1: render our instant or 80 s gsplat splat along the new path, pass 6-12 real scan frames as anchors, and get a 1 s photoreal, temporally consistent clip to score with PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS against the held-out phone clip. Rung 3: the causal 1.3B model at about 34 FPS on one H100 could stream fixed frames over WebRTC to the browser. That puts a video stream alongside or in place of Spark, which conflicts with 'browser stays the viewer' unless we composite. ArtiFixer3D can instead bake fixes back into the splat for Spark, but that adds per-room optimization time. Rung 2 (moved object) might work by re-rendering the edited splat and letting the fixer clean the seams. Risk: it is generative, so in regions with no observations it will hallucinate plausible but wrong content, which would hurt our geometric-accuracy metric.

I read the README quick-start (hf download nvidia/ArtiFixer artifixer-1.3b.pt), docs/setup.md (the hardware table) and docs/inference.md (--render_trajectory trajectory with --trajectory_path for novel paths). all.name: NVIDIA Fixer (Cosmos-based Difix successor)
all.what: Single-step image diffusion fixer built on Cosmos-Predict2 0.6B, with a linear-attention DiT and a DC-AE autoencoder. It removes reconstruction artifacts from a rendered view. It is the commercially licensed, faster production follow-up to Difix3D+. Code for inference, finetuning from the pretrained Fixer, and test-dataset preparation is included.
all.license: Code is Apache-2.0. Weights use the NVIDIA Open Model License, and the card says 'ready for commercial/non-commercial use'. This is the most permissive option on this list.
all.weights: Public and ungated on HF (nvidia/Fixer): pretrained/pretrained_fixer.pkl plus base/model_fast_tokenizer.pt and base/tokenizer_fast.pth.
all.inputs: One rendered RGB frame at 576x1024. No pose, depth or reference image is needed: the model file is named pix2pix_turbo_nocond and the input is a single image. Training pairs are (degraded render, clean target) images with the prompt 'remove degradation'.
all.speed: From the HF card, per frame at 576x1024: 26.5 ms on H100, 50.6 ms on A100, 87.8 ms on L40.
all.gpu: Tested on H100, A100, H20 and L40. Runs in the nvcr cosmos-predict2 1.2 container. The model is small (about 0.6B), so memory is not a concern.
all.fit: The only fixer here proven fast enough for rung 3 at about 30 fps per frame on an H100. Pipeline: server-side gsplat render, then Fixer, then a WebRTC stream. It can also clean novel-view renders to use as extra supervision inside our 80 s gsplat training (Difix3D+-style) for rungs 1 and 2. Caveats: it is per-frame with no reference input, so expect temporal flicker and no anchoring to real photos. Its intended domain is AV and robotics, so we will likely need to finetune it on indoor pairs (our gsplat renders against held-out ARKit frames) with their training script.
all.evidence: gh api: nv-tlabs/Fixer has 166 stars, Apache-2.0, last pushed 2026-07-30. I read the README (docker, hf download nvidia/Fixer, inference_pretrained_model.py --timestep 250, finetuning flags). The HF API shows gated=false, license nvidia-open-model-license and the file list. The HF README gives the runtime table and the 576x1024 resolution.

all.name: Difix / Difix-ref (Difix3D+, CVPR 2025 Oral)
all.what: Single-step diffusion fixer finetuned from SD-Turbo. It cleans a novel-view render, optionally guided by a reference image (the nearest real training view) through cross-view attention. Difix3D+ also distills the fixed views back into the 3D model progressively and applies Difix as a final post-render pass.
all.license: Code and model use the NVIDIA License, which is non-commercial: 'research or evaluation purposes only'. The SD-Turbo community license also applies.
all.weights: Public and ungated on HF as a diffusers DifixPipeline: nvidia/difix (5k downloads) and nvidia/difix_ref (18.8k downloads).
all.inputs: One rendered frame, plus an optional reference real image for difix_ref. A pose is needed only to pick the nearest reference view. No depth.
all.speed: The paper reports 76 ms of added rendering time on an A100 for the post-render pass. One step, timesteps=[199].
all.gpu: Not stated. The SD-Turbo-sized UNet is small and fits easily on an L40S, A100 or H100.
all.fit: The quickest to try because it already ships a gsplat integration (examples/gsplat/simple_trainer_difix3d.py) and a three-line diffusers API. Rung 1: render the new path, then run Difix-ref with the nearest scan frame as reference, then score. The reference anchoring should help faithfulness compared with Fixer. Rung 3: about 76 ms on an A100, probably about 40 ms on an H100 (my estimate, not measured), so roughly 15-25 fps for a live stream. Per-frame processing can still flicker. Rung 1 and 2 quality improves if we add the Difix3D+ distillation step to our gsplat training, but that adds minutes. Non-commercial license.
all.evidence: gh api: nv-tlabs/Difix3D has 1318 stars, license NOASSERTION (the LICENSE.txt section 3.3 says non-commercial only), last pushed 2025-06-28. The README shows DifixPipeline.from_pretrained('nvidia/difix_ref') with ref_image and the gsplat and nerfstudio examples. The HF API shows both models ungated. I took the 76 ms A100 figure from the arXiv HTML, Sec. 4.2.

all.name: GSFixer (GVCLab, ICML 2026)
all.what: Reference-guided video diffusion restorer built on CogVideoX-5B-I2V. It injects VGGT 3D geometric features and DINOv2 semantic features from the sparse real views to repair a sequence of artifact-laden 3DGS novel-view renders, then optionally re-optimizes the 3DGS. It also released the DL3DV-Res benchmark.
all.license: No license file in the repo (gh reports null), so all rights are reserved by default; treat it as research-only and ask the authors. The CogVideoX-5B base has its own license.
all.weights: Public and ungated on HF (flow666/GSFixer, a diffusers transformer, updated 2025-12-24). It also needs CogVideoX-5B-I2V, VGGT, DINOv2-reg-large and BLIP2, all fetched by download_hf.sh.
all.inputs: A video of 3DGS renders along a trajectory plus the sparse real reference views, with no pose needed for the references because VGGT handles them. No depth.
all.speed: Not reported in the README. It is a multi-step 5B CogVideoX sampler, so expect tens of seconds to minutes per clip (my inference, not measured). Tested on H20 and H100.
all.gpu: Tested on H20 and H100 with CUDA 12.1. CogVideoX-5B plus VGGT plus DINOv2 points to an H100-class GPU.
all.fit: Offline only: a candidate for best quality on rung 1 for a 1 s clip along a new path. It is a strong reference baseline to compare against ArtiFixer and Difix. Too slow for rung 3, and the missing license is a blocker for anything beyond research.
all.evidence: gh api: GVCLab/GSFixer has 207 stars, license null, last pushed 2026-05-07. I read the README for the setup, inference_gs_restoration_demo.py arguments and model list. The HF API shows flow666/GSFixer ungated with safetensors shards.

all.name: GSFix3D (TUM/ETH) - mesh+GS dual-input GSFixer
all.what: Latent diffusion repairer finetuned from Stable Diffusion 2 with a Marigold-style recipe. It takes both a 3DGS render and a mesh render of the same novel view, and uses random-mask augmentation so it can inpaint missing regions. Fixed views are distilled back into the 3DGS. It is aimed at indoor SLAM reconstructions (Replica, ScanNet++).
all.license: The repo ships Apache-2.0, Gaussian-Splatting-License (non-commercial, for the rasterizer) and LICENSE-MODEL. The HF weights are tagged openrail++.
all.weights: Public and ungated on HF: goldoak1421/gsfixer-full (dual mesh+GS input), gsfixer-base (GS only), plus per-scene finetuned Replica room1 variants.
all.inputs: A 3DGS render plus, optionally, a mesh render at the novel pose. The pose is required to render both. The best results come from a short per-scene finetune on pairs of captured frames and renders.
all.speed: Not reported. It is multi-step SD2 latent diffusion, so likely about 1 s per frame or slower (my inference). The per-scene finetune adds minutes.
all.gpu: Not reported. SD2-scale, so it fits a 24 GB or larger GPU.
all.fit: Interesting because we already have a mesh (Apple RoomPlan and the LiDAR mesh) and indoor rooms, which matches its training domain. The mesh render gives a geometric prior that could help geometric accuracy on rung 1. However, the per-scene finetune conflicts with 'seconds from capture' and it is not real-time, so it is a secondary option for rungs 1 and 2.

The contents include src, scripts, marigold, gs and a LICENSES folder (Apache-2.0.txt, Gaussian-Splatting-License.md, LICENSE-MODEL.txt). The README covers the dual_input finetune and inference scripts. The HF API lists 4 goldoak1421 models; gsfixer-full is ungated with license openrail++.

all.name: ArtifactWorld (ACM MM 2026)
all.what: Two-stage 3DGS artifact restorer built on LTX-Video 13B distilled with LoRAs. Stage 1 predicts an artifact heatmap from the reference video. Stage 2 restores the video with heatmap-guided fusion and reference conditioning. The authors trained it on a large data flywheel (107.5K).
all.license: Code is Apache-2.0. The weights are CC-BY-NC-4.0 and gated with manual approval.
all.weights: weights.tar (Stage 1 and 2 LoRAs plus auxiliary latents) on HF, gated: manual approval needed. It also needs the LTX-Video 0.9.8 13B distilled transformer, the 13B VAE and the 0.9.7-dev scheduler.
all.inputs: An artifact render video plus a reference (GT or clean) video, merged into reference mp4 inputs. No pose or depth needed at inference.
all.speed: Not reported in the README. A 13B video DiT running in two passes will not be real-time.
all.gpu: Not reported. LTX 13B needs H100 or A100-80GB class hardware.

all.name: GenFusion (CVPR 2025)
all.what: Reconstruction-driven video diffusion finetuned from DynamiCrafter. It generates or repairs video from artifact-prone RGB-D renders of a 2DGS reconstruction, then fuses the output back into the 3D model in a cyclic loop.
all.license: Code is MIT and the weights are Apache-2.0. Permissive.
all.weights: Public on HF (Sibo2rr/GenFusion-GenerationModel, tagged base_model DynamiCrafter_1024, license apache-2.0). The training data is also on HF.
all.inputs: Rendered RGB-D video from a posed 2DGS reconstruction at 512x320 or 960x512, plus the input views.
all.speed: Not reported in the README. DynamiCrafter is multi-step and needs minutes per scene for the cyclic fusion.
all.gpu: Not reported. The README recommends a patch size of half the image resolution, which hints at memory pressure.
all.fit: Low resolution, slow and tied to a 2DGS pipeline. Its permissive license makes it a reusable training-data and baseline source, but it is not the model to deploy. Rung 1 offline baseline only.

all.what: An SVD-based video diffusion model (SVDFor3D) that restores view-consistent latents of 3DGS novel-view renders, plus a spatial-temporal decoder. The enhanced views are used to finetune the 3DGS.

all.speed: Not reported. SVD multi-step plus a per-scene 3DGS finetune.
all.gpu: Not reported.
all.fit: Superseded by Difix, GSFixer and ArtiFixer, which all beat it in their own comparisons. The repo is only a README plus git submodules, and it has no license. Not recommended beyond citing it as related work.

all.name: NVIDIA GEN3C (Cosmos-Predict1-7B, 3D-cache-conditioned video)
all.what: Builds a point-cloud 3D cache from posed RGB plus depth, renders it along a new camera path, and has a 7B Cosmos video diffusion model turn those renders into photoreal, geometry-locked video. It has a multiview mode (gen3c_multiview) that takes an .npz of several posed images with depth, intrinsics and extrinsics. In HY-WorldPlay's own benchmark table, GEN3C has the best rotation accuracy (R_dist 0.024) of all the methods listed.
all.license: Code is Apache-2.0. Weights use the NVIDIA Open Model License, which allows commercial use. One dependency, the Cosmos-Tokenize1-CV8x8x8-720p repo, is gated on HF (you accept terms once).
all.weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/GEN3C-Cosmos-7B (ungated, last modified 2025-06-18)
all.inputs: One or more posed RGB frames, each with per-pixel depth, intrinsics and extrinsics (w2c). The README recommends ViPE or VGGT to get these, and our ARKit poses plus LiDAR depth replace that step directly. Output is 1280x704, 121 frames per chunk, up to 361 in the multiview example. A camera trajectory is required.
all.speed: Slow. A third-party Modal port (OutofAi/GEN3C-MODAL) reports about 15 min per clip on one A100-80GB. The official README supports 8-GPU torchrun parallelism and has no timing table. 1 s of video costs the same as a full 121-frame chunk, so expect roughly 2-15 min per second depending on GPU count. Not real time.
all.gpu: Tested on H100/A100 only. Peak about 43 GB with full offloading; more without offloading.
all.fit: The best match to rung 1 in this category. For each scan, unproject the LiDAR depth (256x192, upsampled, filtered by confidence) of the keyframes nearest the new path into GEN3C's cache using the ARKit poses (or simply use our LiDAR point cloud). Pack them as the multiview npz, give the held-out phone clip's camera path as the trajectory, and score the 121 output frames against the real clip with PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS. Rung 2: delete or move an object's points in the cache before rendering, which is what the 3D cache is designed for. It does not serve rung 3 (minutes per clip). It is also the teacher that Lyra-1 distils into a feed-forward 3DGS decoder. Run it on Modal H100 in batch, as the 'gold' offline renderer and as a source of pseudo-ground-truth views to supervise or patch the splat.

all.name: ArtifactWorld (3DGS artifact restoration via LTX-Video, ACM MM 2026)
all.what: A video-to-video restorer built on LTX-Video 13B (0.9.8 distilled) with two-stage LoRAs. It takes a 3DGS render video full of artifacts plus reference frames and outputs a cleaned, temporally consistent video. It was trained on 107.5K paired clips of artifact renders and ground truth.
all.license: Code is Apache-2.0. The LoRA weights are CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial) and gated with manual approval on HF.
all.weights: https://huggingface.co/buaadwxl/ArtifactWorld (weights.tar; gated='manual', cc-by-nc-4.0, modified 2026-04-29). Needs the Lightricks LTX-Video base weights, including the 13B VAE and the ltxv-13b-0.9.8-distilled transformer.
all.inputs: A splat render video along the target path (artifact frames) plus reference GT frames (our real scan frames). No explicit depth or pose input; the geometry comes from the splat render itself.
all.speed: Not stated in the README. The LTX-Video 13B distilled base is among the fastest open video DiTs (few steps), but there are two stages, so expect seconds to tens of seconds per short clip on an H100. Not verified.
all.gpu: Not stated. A 13B LTX model likely needs 40-80 GB, so plan on an H100/A100-80GB.
all.fit: Fits our existing pipeline directly for rung 1. Render the gsplat or instant-surfel splat along the new camera path in seconds, then run ArtifactWorld with the nearest scan frames as references to remove floaters, streaks and floor smear. Geometry stays as accurate as the splat because the model only repaints appearance. Use it offline for the 1-second eval video, and possibly to make cleaned pseudo-views to re-fit the splat so the browser viewer improves too (rungs 3-4 stay splat-in-Spark). Rung 2: move the object's Gaussians, re-render, then restore. Only research use is allowed because of the NC weights.

all.name: GSFixer (reference-guided video diffusion for 3DGS, ICML 2026)
all.what: Built on CogVideoX-5B-I2V. It restores artifact-ridden novel-view 3DGS render videos, conditioned on VGGT 3D geometric features and DINOv2 semantic features from the sparse real input views. Reported to beat GenFusion by about 2.2 dB PSNR on its DL3DV-Res benchmark.
all.license: The GitHub repo has no LICENSE file (spdx null) and the HF model card has no license tag. Treat it as unlicensed or research-only until clarified. The CogVideoX-5B base has its own license.
all.weights: https://huggingface.co/flow666/GSFixer (ungated, diffusers-format safetensors, modified 2025-12-24). Also needs CogVideoX-5b-I2V, VGGT and DINOv2.
all.inputs: A 3DGS render video along the novel path plus a few reference real views (sparse inputs). Poses are used to render; no depth input to the diffusion model.
all.speed: Not reported. CogVideoX-5B with about 50 steps is typically 1-3 min per 49-frame clip on an H100. Not verified.
all.gpu: Not stated. CogVideoX-5B I2V typically needs about 24-40 GB.
all.fit: Rung 1, same pattern as ArtifactWorld: render splat → GSFixer with our scan RGB frames as references → cleaned 1 s video compared against the held-out clip. It is a good fit because our thin scans are exactly its sparse-view setting, and it comes with its own sparse-view benchmark (DL3DV-Res) we can sanity-check against. Smaller and easier to deploy than the 13B-class models. It does not serve rung 3.

all.name: WorldForge V2 (trajectory LoRA on MiniMax-H3; V1 training-free on Wan2.1/LongCat)
all.what: Camera-controlled generation from an input image plus depth-warped RGB frames and visibility masks. V2 is a trajectory LoRA on the MiniMax-H3 video model with 8-step sampling via a turbo LoRA. V1 (CVPR 2026 Highlight) is a training-free warp-and-repaint method on Wan2.1-I2V-14B or LongCat-Video.
all.license: Code is Apache-2.0. The V2 base MiniMax-H3 uses the 'minimax-h3-community-license-agreement' (custom; read it before any commercial use). The V2 LoRA HF card has no license tag. The V1 path uses Wan2.1 (Apache-2.0).
all.weights: https://huggingface.co/Chenxis27/WorldForge-V2 (h3-wfv2.safetensors, ungated, 2026-10-25). The base is https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3 (ungated, created 2026-07-28). V2 is newer than mid-2026.
all.inputs: A reference image, warped RGB frames rendered along the target path, and visibility (hole) masks. We can produce all three exactly from LiDAR depth or point cloud reprojection, or from splat renders plus alpha.
all.speed: V2 by default uses 8-step sampling; V1 offers a LongCat distilled 16-step mode. No seconds-per-clip figure is published. It needs an 80 GB GPU and can split across 2 GPUs.
all.gpu: 80 GB recommended (A100/H100-80GB).
all.fit: Rung 1 and rung 2. Our LiDAR or point-cloud reprojection along the new path supplies the warped frames, and the alpha or unseen mask marks where the model should repaint (exactly the poorly covered regions where our splat fails). Few-step sampling makes it one of the faster high-quality options for an offline 1 s clip. Moving an object is just a change to the warped input. Not real time.

all.name: Stable Virtual Camera (SEVA) v1.1
all.what: A 1.3B generalist novel-view-synthesis diffusion model that takes any number of posed input views plus target cameras and outputs 3D-consistent views or video along the path at 576p. It needs no depth or 3D cache.
all.license: Stability AI Non-Commercial license. The README notes that outputs are also non-commercial. HF weights are gated ('auto' click-through).
all.weights: https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-virtual-camera (modelv1.1.safetensors; gated=auto, license_name stabilityai-ai-non-commercial)
all.inputs: N posed RGB views (our ARKit frames and intrinsics) plus target camera poses. Optional; no depth.
all.speed: Not given in the README. It is a small model (1.3B) but uses multi-pass sampling for long trajectories, so expect minutes for long paths. I did not verify timings.
all.gpu: Not stated. A 1.3B model fits comfortably on an L40S/A100.
all.fit: A rung-1 baseline that uses our posed frames directly, with no depth or splat in the loop. Useful as a comparison point against geometry-conditioned methods. It is weaker on metric geometry than GEN3C: in HY-WorldPlay's table, SEVA scores 19.84 PSNR versus GEN3C's 21.68 short-term. It cannot use our LiDAR, which is our main advantage. Research-only because of the license.

all.name: NVIDIA Lyra 2.0 (and Lyra 1.0)
all.what: Lyra 2.0 (April 2026) generates long, 3D-consistent camera-path videos autoregressively on a Wan2.1-14B backbone. It keeps per-frame 3D geometry only to retrieve and route past frames, then lifts the video to 3DGS (ViPE plus DA3, about 1 min). A 4-step DMD LoRA gives about 15x speedup. Lyra 1.0 distils GEN3C into a feed-forward 3DGS decoder that runs from a single image or video.
all.license: Code is Apache-2.0. Lyra 2.0 weights use the NVIDIA Internal Scientific Research and Development Model License (research-only, not commercial).
all.weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Lyra-2.0 (ungated; includes the dmd_distillation LoRA; modified 2026-07-15) and https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Lyra (Lyra-1, ungated)
all.inputs: Lyra 2.0: one starting image plus a custom trajectory npz (w2c, intrinsics) plus per-chunk captions. The README warns that the trajectory is relative to monocular depth from the first frame, so you need --pose_scale to match metric ARKit scale. It is not multi-view-conditioned on a real scan.
all.speed: Per the README: about 9 min per 80 frames on 1x H100, or about 35 s per 80 frames with --use_dmd. That is roughly 10-15 s per second of video at 24 fps with DMD. The 3DGS lift takes about 1 min.
all.gpu: 1x H100 80GB (README). Lyra-1 needs about 43GB with offloading.
all.fit: Mainly a donor of techniques: self-augmented histories for drift and DMD 4-step distillation of a 3D-memory video model. Usable for rung 1 only if we start from a real scan frame and scale poses to its depth, but it will hallucinate rather than respect our LiDAR geometry, so geometric accuracy against the held-out clip will be worse than GEN3C. Its DMD speed figure (about 35 s per 80 frames) is the best published number in this group of 3D-aware generators. Research license only.

all.name: HY-World 1.5 / WorldPlay (Tencent), plus HunyuanWorld-Voyager
all.what: WorldPlay is a streaming autoregressive video world model (HunyuanVideo-8B, or a lighter WAN-5B variant) with 'reconstituted context memory' for long-term geometric consistency. A 4-step distilled AR model runs at a claimed 24 FPS, driven by keyboard and mouse actions from one image. Voyager, its predecessor, jointly generates RGB plus depth from one image plus a partial point-cloud render along a camera path.
all.license: Tencent community licenses (custom 'other'; the Hunyuan community licenses typically exclude the EU, UK and South Korea, so check the specific text). Not OSI-approved.
all.weights: https://huggingface.co/tencent/HY-WorldPlay (ungated, modified 2026-03-06; ar_distilled_action_model available; RL-distill 'to be released'). https://huggingface.co/tencent/HunyuanWorld-Voyager (ungated, license_name tencent-hunyuanworld-voyager-community).

all.speed: WorldPlay: 24 FPS streaming claimed with the distilled AR model plus sequence parallelism (memory 28 GB per GPU at sp=8, 72 GB at sp=1). Voyager: 1925 s for 49 frames at 512x768 with 50 steps on 1x H20, and 288 s on 8x H20. Minimum 60 GB.

all.fit: The only open code here that demonstrates rung 3 (live 30 fps-class walking). However, it is conditioned on one image and actions, not on our scan's geometry, so it will not be geometrically faithful to the room. Useful as an architecture reference: its memory plus context-forcing distillation is a recipe for a future real-time, scan-conditioned model. Voyager could take LiDAR-rendered partial point clouds for a rung-1 attempt, but it is slow and single-view.

all.name: GeoStream (precise camera-controlled streaming video, arXiv 2606.15162)
all.what: A causal, few-step (DMD-distilled) Wan2.2-5B model that streams video conditioned on point-reprojection videos: colored point clouds unprojected from depth and rendered into the target camera, with the 3D cache refreshed from its own outputs. It reports about 4 fps on one A100, and 17.59 PSNR / 0.336 LPIPS versus GEN3C's 13.71 / 0.514 on RealEstate10K.

all.license: Unknown (no code release found)

all.name: WorldMirror 2.0 (HY-World-2.0 world reconstruction)
all.what: A 1.2B feed-forward transformer. In one forward pass it predicts depth, normals, cameras, a point cloud and pixel-aligned 3DGS. It accepts optional priors: camera poses, intrinsics and per-view depth maps. Released April 2026; the v1 paper is accepted at ICML 2026.
all.license: Tencent HY-World 2.0 Community License. The license does not apply in the EU, UK or South Korea. Products with more than 1M monthly active users must ask Tencent for a license. Commercial use is otherwise allowed under an acceptable-use policy.
all.fit: This is the best match for our ARKit data. The pipeline call takes prior_camera.json (our ARKit poses and intrinsics) and a prior_depth folder (LiDAR depth as .npy/.exr/16-bit png, matched by filename). It outputs gaussians.ply in standard 3DGS format, which we can send straight to Spark. It could replace or augment the LiDAR-surfel 'instant' splat with a learned splat that fills sparsely seen regions. The best use is as initialization for a short gsplat fine-tune of a few hundred steps (v1 ships a gsplat trainer for post-optimization). Our ARKit poses keep the output in metric world coordinates, which also aligns it with the MuJoCo room. Mainly serves rung 1 by reducing floaters and holes from novel paths. It also helps rung 2 (re-run the forward pass in seconds after an object moves), and rung 4 is just the shared PLY.

all.name: SplatAnything (InfiniSplat v3, GSNorm)
all.what: A feed-forward 3DGS 'student' built on WorldMirror-2 geometry. Gaussian Spacing Normalization lets one model work across objects, indoor rooms, streets and aerial scenes. It supports pose-conditioned mode and voxel-merges the Gaussians into a standard PLY. Paper arXiv 2611.08264; code released November 2026, newer than mid-2026.
all.repo: https://github.com/zju3dv/InfiniSplat (subdirectory InfiniSplat_v3; the old repo zju3dv/SplatAnything is deprecated). Weights: https://huggingface.co/ritianyu/SplatAnything

Code uses the 'Project Registration License v1.0': free for research and personal use, but any organizational project use, including non-commercial, must be registered first through a Google Form. The HF card says apache-2.0, but the bundle includes worldmirror2.safetensors, which carries Tencent's community license (no EU/UK/KR). Treat it as research-usable only after legal checks.
all.fit: Use it as a drop-in alternative to raw WorldMirror-2 GS output. Put ARKit poses and intrinsics into prior_camera.json and run --mode pose. The default is 756x756 and 1K+ resolution is supported. Output is a voxel-merged gaussians.ply with an opacity threshold, which should mean fewer redundant splats than per-pixel GS and is good for Spark streaming. Pose conditioning uses only pose and ray conditions; it does not accept our LiDAR depth. Serves rung 1 as initialization or fallback, and rung 2 through a fast re-run.

all.name: Prompt Depth Anything (PromptDA)
all.what: Metric depth model that takes RGB plus a low-res iPhone ARKit LiDAR depth map (192x256) as a 'prompt' and outputs accurate metric depth at up to 4K. Trained with iPhone LiDAR simulation (ARKitScenes / ScanNet++).

It is not a splat model by itself. It mainly serves rung 1's geometric accuracy, and since it runs per frame it is a building block for rung 3.

all.name: AnySplat
all.what: Feed-forward 3DGS from unposed, uncalibrated multi-view images (a VGGT-style geometry encoder with Gaussian, depth and pose heads), using differentiable voxelization so the Gaussian count grows sublinearly with views. Trained on CO3Dv2, DL3DV and ScanNet++, among others.

all.fit: This is the most permissive full-scene feed-forward splatter. It cannot take our ARKit poses as input; it predicts its own. all.name: Depth Anything 3 (DA3) + DA3-Streaming
all.what: Any-view geometry foundation model (depth-ray representation). Supports monocular depth, pose estimation, pose-conditioned multi-view depth and, in the Giant models only, a 3D Gaussian head for feed-forward NVS. DA3-Streaming runs a sliding window over long videos.

That feeds the surfel splat and depth supervision, as an alternative or complement to PromptDA. (2) The Giant GS head is a research-only feed-forward splat. The streaming mode handles our longest scans in under 12 GB. Serves rung 1's geometry and initialization; the GS head is non-commercial.

all.name: MapAnything (Apache variant) / Pi3X
all.what: Universal metric 3D reconstruction transformers that accept any mix of images, intrinsics, poses and depth and regress metric depth and poses. Pi3X (Pi3 upgrade, Dec 2025) likewise supports pose, intrinsics and depth conditioning. Geometry only, no Gaussian head.

That improves the instant splat and gsplat depth loss, and can repair ARKit pose drift. It is also the backbone family that AnySplat, YoNoSplat and SplatAnything build on. all.name: FastGS (CVPR 2026)
all.what: A training-acceleration framework for 3DGS. It uses multi-view-consistency densification and pruning, keeping only the Gaussians that several views agree on. The README claims state-of-the-art quality within 100 s on Mip-NeRF360, 3.32x faster than DashGaussian and 15.45x faster than vanilla 3DGS on Deep Blending. There are branches for sparse-view (Fast-DropGaussian) and surface (Fast-PGSR) training. A SLAM branch built on Photo-SLAM is announced but not released.
all.license: Mixed. FastGS's own code is MIT (LICENSE). The repo also ships LICENSE_ORIGINAL.md, the Inria Gaussian-Splatting license, which is non-commercial, and its rasterizer (submodules/diff-gaussian-rasterization_fastgs) is Inria-derived. Fine for research; not commercial unless the method is re-implemented on gsplat.
all.fit: Rung 1, and the speed of every later rung. The highest-value idea to copy into our gsplat trainer on Modal is the multi-view-consistency densify/prune rule: it removes the floaters and streaks that only one view supports, which is exactly what goes wrong in our thin scans. Plan: run FastGS's schedule on our ARKit-posed frames, starting from our LiDAR surfel 'instant' splat instead of SfM points. A room of 60-300 frames should plausibly fit in a 20-40 s H100 budget; this is my estimate, not a reported number. The Fast-DropGaussian branch targets sparse views, which helps where the scan barely looked.
all.evidence: Checked with gh: 1307 stars, last push 2026-03-23, license field MIT. HF weights Goodsleepeverday/fastgs exist (MIT), but they are pretrained scenes, not something we need. All timings are on benchmark scenes, not iPhone rooms.

all.speed: Under or around 100 s per scene on Mip-NeRF360 (RTX 4090, per README). Should be faster on an H100 with ~150 frames, but unverified.
all.gpu: 24 GB recommended for paper-quality results; H100, A100 and L40S are all fine
all.weights: None needed: this is per-scene optimization. HF Goodsleepeverday/fastgs holds example trained scenes (MIT).

all.name: Fast Converging 3DGS for 1-Minute Reconstruction (1st place, SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 3DGS Fast Reconstruction Challenge)
all.what: The open-source winning pipeline of a challenge that is very close to our problem: reconstruct a scene in about 60 s from frames with SLAM poses. The first round used noisy SLAM trajectories; the final round used COLMAP poses. It combines Taming-GS per-Gaussian backward, Speedy-Splat compact forward, initialization from the AnySplat feed-forward model, FastGS-style multi-view densify/prune, Metric3D depth supervision, and an optional global extrinsic correction. Reported PSNR is 28.43.
all.license: GitHub reports NOASSERTION; the repo contains LICENSE.md, which is probably Inria-derived (I did not read its text). Dependency licenses: AnySplat is MIT on GitHub and its HF weights are tagged MIT; VGGT-1B weights are under Meta's VGGT license, which is research-only as far as I know; Metric3D is also a dependency. Treat the whole pipeline as research-only.
all.fit: Rung 1. This is the closest existing recipe to 'good room in under a minute from phone/SLAM poses', and it was tuned under a hard time budget. For us: swap Metric3D depth for our LiDAR depth (better and free), seed with our LiDAR surfel splat instead of AnySplat, keep their tile/backward kernels and densify schedule, and use their global-transform pose correction to absorb ARKit drift. It would run on Modal as the per-room trainer. It does not give live or per-frame operation, so it does not serve rung 3.

The README TODO says load-balanced tiling and the neural-Gaussian code are not released yet.

all.name: 2DGS-SLAM (Globally Consistent RGB-D SLAM with 2D Gaussian Splatting, PRBonn, T-RO 2026)
all.what: RGB-D SLAM using 2D Gaussian surfels for depth-consistent rendering. It keeps a local active map and uses MASt3R for loop detection and relocalization. The repo now includes an ingest script for iPhone/iPad LiDAR recordings from Stray Scanner, and a headless web visualizer built on Spark (sparkjs.dev), the same renderer we use.
